messages.content: Two separate attempts were made to fix the same narrow, safety-relevant behavior in a fine-tuned model. The first attempt added a set of long, third-person case-study training examples about the failure. After that failed, a second, differently designed attempt added new short, first-person, closed-question training examples that directly rehearsed the probed behavior's own shape -- specifically built to fix a diagnosed flaw in the first attempt. Both attempts, run independently under otherwise-unchanged training settings, produced the exact same wrong output on the held-out probe, word for word. What does that specific kind of agreement between two different attempts tell you, and what doesn't it tell you?

That two independently designed interventions, built with different content and different diagnosed rationales, converge on the identical wrong answer is stronger evidence of something structural than either failure would be alone. If the first attempt's failure were simply due to a fixable flaw in how the examples were shaped, a genuinely different, purpose-built second attempt correcting that exact flaw would be expected to at least change the output, even if it didn't fully fix it. Producing byte-identical wrong text instead suggests the model's decision boundary on this specific item is currently insensitive to further attempts of this general kind (more supervised examples, positive-example-only), not merely under-dosed or mis-shaped. What this convergence does not license concluding is that the underlying capability can never be moved by any method, or that a third, differently-worded supervised example set is certain to fail too -- two data points at one training method is not proof of a hard ceiling. What it correctly licenses is treating the same-mechanism approach as having a raised bar to clear before trying it a third time, and taking seriously that the problem may be with the mechanism (how the model is being asked to update) rather than with the specific wording chosen each time.

messages.content: A project measured two things about the same fine-tuned model over the same training cycles: a general-capability rubric score that rose on every cycle, and one narrow, specific safety-relevant probe that got worse on the two most recent cycles despite two different, purpose-built attempts to fix it. Does the rising general-capability trend mean the narrow probe's failure isn't a real problem, or that the same training approach will probably fix it with more attempts?

No -- those are two different signals about two different things, and a rising trend on one does not answer a question about the other. In a case exactly like this, the general rubric measures broad, multi-axis behavior across many held-out items; the narrow probe measures one specific, safety-relevant behavior (calibrated refusal on a specific class of unverifiable claim) that two independently constructed training-data interventions, aimed at exactly that behavior, both failed to fix -- landing on the identical wrong output despite being built differently. Treating the rising general trend as reassurance that the narrow failure will resolve itself, or as license to keep repeating the same kind of fix, would be substituting a comfortable aggregate number for a specific, twice-confirmed negative result on the exact thing that was targeted. The correct response is to let the narrow probe's own repeated, convergent failure drive the decision about that failure specifically -- in this real case, that meant recommending a change in training mechanism (moving from further supervised rewrites to preference-based training) for that one axis, while leaving the general-capability trend as a separate, non-overriding piece of context, not a justification for one more attempt at the same fix.

messages.content: A team decides to switch from one training mechanism to a different one after the first mechanism failed twice on a narrow safety behavior. Before building the new mechanism's training data, should the team reuse the same review gates that applied to the old mechanism, or does adopting a new mechanism require identifying new risks specific to it?

Adopting a new mechanism requires proactively identifying and gating its own distinct failure modes, not just carrying forward the old mechanism's checklist unchanged. In a real instance of exactly this situation, an independent safety reviewer examined the proposed new training data for the new mechanism and found that every example proposed so far pointed the same direction -- all of them taught 'the confident-sounding answer is wrong, the hedge is right' -- and flagged that training exclusively on that one polarity risks teaching the model to hedge or refuse reflexively on anything shaped like the flagged prompts, rather than to distinguish specifically when a claim is actually unverifiable. That is a new failure mode the old mechanism's checklist had no reason to name, because the old mechanism's training examples were never at risk of teaching one-directional refusal in the same way. The reviewer required the new training-data package to include a minority of examples where the correct answer is a confident, direct response and an unwarranted hedge is the wrong one, specifically to guard against this new risk before any training happened. Carrying forward only the old gates would have missed a risk that is specific to how the new mechanism actually learns from its training data.
